title: Deploying to the cloud
intro: Getting an application onto the internet involves more than building a Docker image: you need hosting, configuration, secrets, database migrations, health checks, and a safe way to release new versions. In this lesson, you will learn how to deploy a React frontend and Spring Boot backend using common cloud architectures while keeping configuration and production concerns separate from your code.
body:
## What deploying to the cloud means

A production application needs somewhere to run. When people say that an application is deployed "to the cloud", they usually mean that the application runs on infrastructure provided by a cloud or hosting provider rather than directly on a developer's computer.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "A typical production setup", "nodes": [{"id": "u", "label": "Users", "kind": "user"}, {"id": "cdn", "label": "CDN / static host", "sub": "React build · HTTPS", "kind": "cloud", "highlight": true}, {"id": "api", "label": "API container", "sub": "PaaS · APP_PROFILE=prod", "kind": "server", "highlight": true}, {"id": "db", "label": "Managed PostgreSQL", "sub": "backups · TLS", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "sec", "label": "Secrets", "sub": "env vars in the platform", "kind": "file", "col": 1}], "edges": [{"from": "u", "to": "cdn", "label": "shop.example.com"}, {"from": "cdn", "to": "api", "label": "api.example.com"}, {"from": "api", "to": "db", "label": "DATABASE_URL"}, {"from": "sec", "to": "api", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

There is no single correct cloud architecture for every project. A small application might use a static frontend host, a managed backend platform, and a managed PostgreSQL database. A larger company might use Kubernetes, multiple regions, private networks, and dedicated infrastructure.

For the full-stack application from this course, a simple production architecture could be:

~~~text
                    Internet
                       |
                Custom domain + HTTPS
                       |
              +--------+--------+
              |                 |
              v                 v
        React static site    Spring Boot API
          CDN / hosting       PaaS / VPS
                                  |
                                  v
                         Managed PostgreSQL
~~~

The important thing is to separate responsibilities. The frontend serves static files. The backend runs application logic. PostgreSQL stores persistent data. Each component can then be scaled, updated, or replaced independently.

---

## Choosing where to host the frontend

A production Vite React application is ultimately a collection of static files after `npm run build` finishes.

That means you often do not need a traditional server to host the frontend. A CDN-backed static hosting platform can serve the generated HTML, JavaScript, CSS, and assets from locations close to users.

Common choices include platforms such as Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages.

A typical deployment looks like:

~~~text
npm ci
npm run build
       |
       v
      dist/
       |
       v
Static hosting / CDN
~~~

Static hosting is attractive because the infrastructure required to serve files is relatively simple. You do not need to maintain a Linux server, install nginx manually, or manage a Node.js process for the production frontend.

The main thing to remember is that the browser still needs to know where the backend API lives. That leads to an important production configuration value such as `VITE_API_URL`.

---

## Choosing where to host the backend

A Spring Boot backend needs a runtime environment capable of running the application.

There are three broad options that make sense for a small application.

### Platform as a Service

A PaaS provider manages much of the infrastructure for you. Examples include Render, Fly.io, and Railway.

You typically provide a Git repository or container image and configure environment variables. The platform then builds or starts your application and exposes it through a public URL.

This is often the easiest starting point because you can concentrate on the application rather than maintaining the operating system.

### VPS

A **virtual private server (VPS)** gives you more direct control over a Linux server. You can install Docker, configure nginx or another reverse proxy, manage certificates, and run your Compose stack yourself.

This can be inexpensive and flexible, but you become responsible for more operational work:

- Operating system updates.
- Firewall configuration.
- Docker updates.
- Backups.
- Monitoring.
- TLS configuration.
- Log management.
- Recovery when something fails.

### Managed application infrastructure

Larger applications may use managed container platforms, orchestration systems, or cloud services that provide automated scaling and deployment.

For a first production application, however, complexity is usually better added only when there is a real requirement for it.

---

## Managed PostgreSQL

You generally should not treat the production database as an ordinary disposable container on the same machine as your application unless you have a specific reason and a proper backup strategy.

A managed PostgreSQL service can handle many operational tasks for you, such as:

- Database provisioning.
- Automated backups.
- Updates and maintenance.
- Monitoring.
- High availability options.
- Storage management.

Your Spring Boot application then receives a database connection configuration through an environment variable.

For example:

~~~text
DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db.example.com:5432/shop
~~~

The exact connection format depends on the hosting provider and application configuration.

The important principle is that the database connection is configuration, not source code.

---

## Twelve-factor configuration

Production configuration should not be hard-coded into the application.

The **twelve-factor application** approach popularized the idea of storing configuration that varies between environments outside the codebase, commonly through environment variables.

For example, your development environment might use:

~~~text
APP_PROFILE=dev
DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173
~~~

Production might use:

~~~text
APP_PROFILE=prod
DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://production-db.example.com:5432/shop
CORS_ORIGINS=https://shop.example.com
~~~

The same application artifact can then run in both environments with different configuration.

This is a major benefit of containers and CI/CD. You can build an image once and configure it differently when it is deployed.

---

## Spring profiles

Spring Boot provides **profiles** for environment-specific configuration.

A common setup is:

~~~text
src/main/resources/
├── application.yml
└── application-prod.yml
~~~

The default configuration can contain shared settings, while `application-prod.yml` contains production-specific Spring configuration.

For example:

~~~yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    show-sql: false
  flyway:
    enabled: true
~~~

The production profile can be selected with an environment variable:

~~~text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
~~~

Your application can also use a custom variable such as `APP_PROFILE` and translate it into the Spring profile configuration used by the application.

The important architectural distinction is that profile files should not become a place to store production passwords or API keys. Configuration structure can live in source control; secrets should be supplied securely at runtime.

---

## Secrets must stay out of Git

A database password, JWT signing secret, API key, or cloud credential is a **secret**.

Do not write production secrets into:

~~~text
application-prod.yml
compose.yaml
Dockerfile
source code
GitHub workflow files
~~~

Instead, use the secret-management facilities provided by the environment.

For example, your production platform might provide:

~~~text
DATABASE_URL=...
JWT_SECRET=...
CORS_ORIGINS=https://shop.example.com
~~~

The application reads these values at startup.

A `.env` file can be convenient for local development, but it should not automatically be treated as secure production secret storage. A local `.env` containing credentials should normally be excluded from Git.

If a secret is accidentally committed, simply deleting it in a later commit is not enough. The secret should be considered compromised and rotated.

---

## The frontend API URL

A React frontend needs to know which backend it should call.

With Vite, variables intended for client-side code commonly use the `VITE_` prefix.

For example:

~~~text
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
~~~

The application might use it like this:

~~~typescript
const apiUrl = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;

fetch(`${apiUrl}/api/products`);
~~~

There is an important security detail here: **Vite environment variables exposed to browser code are not secrets**.

Anything included in the frontend bundle can eventually be inspected by a user. Therefore, `VITE_API_URL` is appropriate for a public API URL, but a JWT signing secret or database password must never use a `VITE_` variable.

A useful rule is:

~~~text
Frontend configuration -> public if bundled into JavaScript
Backend secrets       -> private server-side configuration
~~~

---

## CORS in production

During development, your frontend and backend may run on different origins:

~~~text
Frontend: http://localhost:5173
Backend:  http://localhost:8080
~~~

The browser's same-origin policy prevents arbitrary cross-origin requests unless the backend explicitly allows them.

This is where **CORS**, or Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, comes in.

In production, you might have:

~~~text
Frontend: https://shop.example.com
Backend:  https://api.example.com
~~~

The backend should allow the actual frontend origin:

~~~text
CORS_ORIGINS=https://shop.example.com
~~~

Avoid using `*` for production origins when your authentication and security model requires a restricted set of trusted origins.

CORS is enforced by browsers. It is not an authentication mechanism. Allowing an origin does not mean that the user is authenticated or authorized to perform an operation.

---

## Database migrations with Flyway

When you deploy a new version of the backend, the database schema may also need to change.

For example, version 2 might add a product description column. You do not want developers or operators to manually edit the production database every time the application changes.

Flyway provides versioned database migrations.

A migration might be named something like:

~~~text
V3__add_product_description.sql
~~~

When the application starts, Flyway checks which migrations have already been applied and executes pending migrations in order.

A typical deployment can therefore look like:

~~~text
Deploy new application
        |
        v
Spring Boot starts
        |
        v
Flyway checks migrations
        |
        v
Pending migrations run
        |
        v
Application becomes ready
~~~

This is particularly useful in automated deployments because the database schema changes become part of the versioned application lifecycle.

Production migrations still require care. A destructive migration can break an older application version that is still running during a zero-downtime deployment. Prefer backward-compatible database changes when old and new application versions may temporarily coexist.

---

## Health checks and readiness

A process being alive does not necessarily mean the application is ready.

Spring Boot Actuator can expose health information through:

~~~text
/actuator/health
~~~

A platform can use this endpoint to determine whether the application is healthy enough to receive traffic.

For example:

~~~text
Start new instance
      |
      v
Application starts
      |
      v
Flyway completes
      |
      v
/actuator/health -> UP
      |
      v
Receive traffic
~~~

This distinction is important for safe deployments. If the platform sends traffic to a container while Spring Boot is still starting, users may receive errors even though the process itself is technically running.

Health endpoints should also be designed carefully. They should provide enough information for the infrastructure to determine readiness without unnecessarily exposing sensitive internal details to the public internet.

---

## Zero-downtime deployments

A **zero-downtime deployment** means that users should continue to receive service while a new application version is being released.

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "A rolling, zero-downtime deploy", "steps": [{"label": "Start v2", "sub": "next to v1"}, {"label": "Migrate", "sub": "backward-compatible only"}, {"label": "Readiness OK", "sub": "/actuator/health/readiness"}, {"label": "Switch traffic", "sub": "v1 drains"}, {"label": "Stop v1", "sub": "keep it for rollback"}]}
~~~

One simple strategy is to start a new instance while the existing version is still serving traffic:

~~~text
Version A -> serving traffic
Version B -> starting
Version B -> healthy
Version A + B -> traffic transition
Version A -> removed
~~~

The exact implementation depends on the hosting platform. A PaaS may handle this automatically. With a VPS, you may implement it using a reverse proxy and multiple application instances.

Zero-downtime deployments create an important compatibility requirement: the old and new versions may temporarily run at the same time.

That affects database migrations. For example, immediately removing a database column while the old application still expects it can break requests.

A safer pattern is often:

1. Add the new database structure.
2. Deploy code that can work with both old and new structures.
3. Switch traffic to the new application version.
4. Remove obsolete structures later.

This is sometimes called an expand-and-contract migration strategy.

---

## Rollbacks

A deployment is not successful simply because the new container starts.

You should also be able to return to the previous known-good version if production behaviour is incorrect.

A release process should therefore produce identifiable artifacts:

~~~text
release-42
commit-a1b2c3d
image: ghcr.io/example/shop-api:a1b2c3d
~~~

If version 43 introduces a serious problem, the platform can return to version 42.

Database changes complicate rollbacks. Application code can often be rolled back quickly, but a migration that permanently removes data may not be reversible.

This is another reason to design database migrations conservatively and maintain reliable backups.

---

## Custom domains and HTTPS

Users expect production applications to use a real domain and HTTPS.

You might have:

~~~text
https://shop.example.com
https://api.example.com
~~~

The domain's DNS records point to the appropriate hosting infrastructure.

HTTPS encrypts traffic between the client and server and also provides server identity through TLS certificates.

Modern hosting platforms often provision and renew certificates automatically once DNS is configured correctly. On a self-managed VPS, you need to configure certificate issuance and renewal yourself.

Do not treat HTTPS as optional for an application handling authentication, sessions, personal data, or payment-related workflows.

Also make sure your production frontend uses HTTPS when calling an HTTPS backend. Browsers can block insecure mixed-content requests from a secure page.

---

## A practical deployment architecture

For the course webshop, a relatively simple production setup could be:

~~~text
                    DNS
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |                     |
          v                     v
shop.example.com        api.example.com
          |                     |
          v                     v
    Static hosting          Spring Boot
       + CDN                  container
                                |
                                v
                       Managed PostgreSQL
~~~

The React application is built by CI and uploaded to the static hosting provider.

The Spring Boot Docker image is built by CI and published to a container registry. The PaaS or VPS deploys that image.

The PostgreSQL database is managed separately and is configured through an environment variable.

This architecture avoids running unnecessary infrastructure yourself while still giving you a clear separation between frontend, backend, and data.

---

## A deployment checklist

Before calling a deployment complete, verify the following.

~~~callout tip Before you press Deploy
- CI is green on `main`
- New migrations are backward compatible
- Secrets are set in the platform, not in Git
- `CORS_ORIGINS` and `VITE_API_URL` point to production
- You know the command to roll back
~~~

### Application

- The production build succeeds.
- Backend tests pass.
- Frontend tests pass.
- The Docker image starts successfully.
- The application listens on the expected port.

### Configuration

- The production Spring profile is active.
- `DATABASE_URL` points to the production database.
- `VITE_API_URL` points to the production API.
- CORS allows the real frontend origin.
- Production secrets are supplied securely.
- No secrets are committed to Git.

### Database

- Flyway migrations are enabled.
- Migrations have been tested against a production-like database.
- Backups exist and recovery has been considered.
- Migrations are compatible with the deployment strategy.

### Operations

- `/actuator/health` reports healthy status.
- Logs are accessible.
- The deployment can be rolled back.
- The application has a custom domain.
- HTTPS is enabled.
- DNS configuration is correct.

### Security

- The application does not run unnecessarily as root.
- Database ports are not publicly exposed without a reason.
- CORS is restricted appropriately.
- Secrets are not present in client-side code.
- CI and hosting credentials use the minimum required permissions.

---

## Common mistakes

### Hard-coding production URLs

Hard-coding a database or API URL makes it difficult to run the same artifact in multiple environments. Use environment-specific configuration instead.

### Treating frontend variables as secrets

Anything exposed through a `VITE_` variable becomes part of the browser application. Users can inspect it. Never put private credentials there.

### Allowing every CORS origin

Using a wildcard origin can be convenient during development but is often too permissive for a production application. Configure the actual frontend origins you trust.

### Deploying without database migration planning

Application code and database schema are connected. A deployment that ignores migrations can leave the application unable to start or produce runtime errors.

### Checking only whether the process is running

A healthy deployment should verify application readiness. Actuator health checks can provide a useful signal for the hosting platform.

### Having no rollback plan

A deployment can succeed technically and still introduce a serious application bug. Keep previous artifacts available and know how to return to a known-good version.

### Putting everything on one VPS without backups

A single server can be perfectly reasonable for a small project, but it also becomes a single point of failure. Backups and recovery procedures matter even for small applications.

---

## From local development to production

You have now covered the path from application code to a production deployment:

~~~text
React + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL
              |
              v
        Docker images
              |
              v
        GitHub Actions
              |
              v
       Container registry
              |
              v
       Cloud / VPS / PaaS
              |
              v
   HTTPS + domain + monitoring
~~~

There is no requirement to start with a complicated cloud architecture. For a small application, a static frontend host, a managed PostgreSQL database, and a simple Spring Boot container platform can be enough.

The important professional skill is understanding the responsibilities involved: configuration, secrets, networking, migrations, health, security, releases, and recovery.

Once you can deploy the application repeatedly and safely, you have moved beyond simply writing software. You are operating software in an environment where real users depend on it.
takeaways: Choose hosting based on how much infrastructure you want to manage: static hosting, PaaS, VPS, and managed databases each have different trade-offs.
Keep environment-specific configuration outside the application artifact and never expose backend secrets through Vite frontend variables.
Use Spring profiles, environment variables, and secure secret storage to separate development and production configuration.
Flyway migrations and health checks should be part of the deployment lifecycle.
Zero-downtime deployments require compatible application and database changes because old and new versions may temporarily coexist.
Every production deployment should have HTTPS, backups, observable health, traceable artifacts, and a rollback strategy.

quiz.question: Why is a static hosting platform often a good fit for a production Vite React frontend?
options: The production build consists mainly of static files that can be efficiently served by a CDN
It provides a PostgreSQL database automatically
React requires a Java server in production
It keeps all frontend code private from users
quiz.explanation: After Vite builds the application, the frontend consists of static assets that can be served efficiently from CDN-backed static hosting.

quiz.question: Why should a production database URL normally be supplied through environment configuration?
options: Because PostgreSQL cannot be used from Java code
Because environment variables automatically encrypt every value
Because the same application artifact can use different databases in different environments without changing source code
Because Spring Boot only supports environment variables
quiz.explanation: Environment-based configuration allows the same application artifact to run against development, staging, or production infrastructure without hard-coding environment-specific values.

quiz.question: Why should a value such as `VITE_API_URL` not contain a JWT signing secret?
options: Vite cannot read variables beginning with VITE_
Values exposed to Vite frontend code become available to browser users
JWT secrets can only be stored in PostgreSQL
Browsers cannot make HTTPS requests
quiz.explanation: Vite variables used by client-side code are bundled into the frontend and can be inspected by users. They are suitable for public configuration such as an API URL, not secrets.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of `/actuator/health` in a deployment?
options: To permanently store application logs
To perform database migrations
To generate JWT tokens
To provide a health or readiness signal that infrastructure can use
quiz.explanation: A health endpoint gives the hosting platform a way to determine whether the application is healthy enough to receive traffic.

quiz.question: Why can database migrations complicate zero-downtime deployments?
options: Because old and new application versions may temporarily run against the same database schema
Because HTTPS prevents Flyway from running
Because Docker containers cannot connect to PostgreSQL
Because static frontends cannot use databases
quiz.explanation: During a rolling or zero-downtime deployment, old and new application versions can coexist. Database changes therefore need to remain compatible with both versions during the transition.

exercise.title: Validate and safely redact production configuration
exercise.task:
Define exactly these two functions:

1. `function loadConfig(env: Record<string, string | undefined>)` — return an object with exactly these properties: `{ port: number, databaseUrl: string, corsOrigins: string[], profile: "dev" | "prod", jwtSecret: string }`.
   - `PORT` defaults to `8080` when it is missing. Otherwise it must represent an integer from 1 through 65535.
   - `DATABASE_URL` is required and must start with `"jdbc:postgresql://"`.
   - `CORS_ORIGINS` is a comma-separated list. Trim each entry, remove empty entries, and default to an empty array when it is missing.
   - `APP_PROFILE` defaults to `"dev"` and must be exactly `"dev"` or `"prod"`.
   - `JWT_SECRET` is required. When the profile is `"prod"`, it must contain at least 32 characters.
   - In `prod`, `corsOrigins` must not contain `"*"`.
   - Collect ALL validation problems before throwing. Throw exactly one `Error` whose message starts with `"Invalid config:"` and contains the individual problems joined with `"; "`. Each problem must name the relevant variable, for example `"DATABASE_URL is required"`.
   - If the configuration is valid, return the parsed configuration.

2. `function redact(config)` — return a copy of the configuration without mutating the input. Replace `jwtSecret` with `"***"`. In `databaseUrl`, replace the password value after `password=` with `"***"`. Preserve the rest of the URL and all other configuration values.

The functions must work for different valid and invalid environments and must not rely on a single hard-coded configuration.
exercise.hint: Validate every independent rule before throwing so you can collect multiple problems. Keep `port` at 8080 unless a valid PORT is supplied. Build `corsOrigins` with split, trim, and filter. Check the profile before applying the production-only JWT and CORS rules. For `redact`, create a new object and replace the password portion with a regular expression that preserves `password=` and stops at the next `&` or the end of the URL.

tests.name: It loads a valid development configuration and applies defaults
It parses a valid production configuration
It rejects invalid ports
It rejects a missing or invalid database URL
It trims CORS origins and removes empty entries
It rejects an invalid application profile
It rejects a missing JWT secret
It applies the production JWT length rule
It rejects a wildcard CORS origin in production
It collects multiple configuration problems in one error
It redacts the JWT secret and database password without mutating the input
